facts.statement: Disability and accidental death or dismemberment provisions are excluded from the 2-year incontestable requirement.
facts.quote: (exclusive of provisions of the policy or any contract supplemental thereto relating to disability benefits or to additional benefits in event of death by accident or accidental means or in event of dismemberment or loss of sight)

items.stem: New Jersey's required 2-year incontestable provision does NOT have to apply to which part of a life policy?
options: An accidental death and dismemberment rider
items.explanation: N.J.S.A. 17B:25-4 excludes provisions on disability benefits and on additional benefits for accidental death, dismemberment or loss of sight from the incontestable requirement.

facts.statement: A waiver of premium rider lets the owner stop paying premiums if the insured develops a covered illness or disability named in the rider.
facts.quote: With a waiver of premium rider, you can stop paying your life insurance premium if you develop a covered illness or disability named in the rider.

items.stem: An insured becomes disabled by a condition named in a rider. The policy stays in force, and the owner owes nothing to the insurer while the disability lasts. Which rider is at work?
items.explanation: Per the NAIC Consumer Guide: Life Insurance Riders, a waiver of premium rider lets you stop paying premiums if you develop a covered illness or disability named in the rider.

facts.statement: An accidental death benefit rider pays more than the death benefit, sometimes two or three times (double or triple indemnity), if death is accidental.
facts.quote: Some riders pay two to three times the death benefit for certain accidents. Insurers sometimes describe these riders as double or triple indemnity.

items.stem: A $100,000 policy has a double indemnity rider. The insured dies in a car accident that the rider covers. The beneficiary receives:
items.explanation: Per the NAIC Consumer Guide: Life Insurance Riders, an accidental death benefit rider, sometimes called double or triple indemnity, pays a multiple of the death benefit for covered accidents. Double indemnity on $100,000 pays $200,000.

facts.statement: A guaranteed insurability rider lets the owner increase the death benefit at set future times without a medical exam; the cost depends on age and the amount of the increase, not health.
facts.quote: How much it costs to increase the benefit will depend on your age and the amount of the increase, not your health or lifestyle.

items.stem: A client with a guaranteed insurability rider develops a serious illness, then reaches one of the rider's option dates and buys more coverage. The premium for the added coverage is based on:
options: How old he is and how much coverage he adds
His current health and medical history
The premium rate set when the policy was issued
A medical exam taken on the option date
items.explanation: Per the NAIC Consumer Guide: Life Insurance Riders, a guaranteed insurability rider allows increases at set times without a medical exam, and the cost depends on age and the amount of the increase, not health or lifestyle.

facts.statement: A long-term care rider lets the insured use part of the death benefit for long-term care, usually triggered by inability to perform certain activities of daily living.
facts.quote: Usually, you must be unable to do certain activities of daily living.

items.stem: A long-term care rider on a life policy usually pays out when the insured:
options: Is diagnosed with any illness that shortens life expectancy
Needs help with basic tasks such as bathing or dressing
items.explanation: Per the NAIC Consumer Guide: Life Insurance Riders, a long-term care rider lets the insured use part of the death benefit for long-term care, and usually requires being unable to do certain activities of daily living.

facts.statement: Money taken under an accelerated death benefit for a terminal illness does not have to be used for care related to the illness.
facts.quote: You don't have to use the money to pay for care related to your illness.

items.stem: A terminally ill insured receives an accelerated death benefit and wants to use it for a family trip. Under a typical accelerated benefit rider, this is:
options: Not allowed, since the money is reserved for medical bills
Allowed, but limited to nursing home costs
Allowed, since the money need not go toward care
Not allowed until the beneficiary consents
items.explanation: Per the NAIC Consumer Guide: Life Insurance Riders, an accelerated death benefit lets a terminally ill insured take money from the death benefit, and the money does not have to be used for care related to the illness.

facts.statement: A rider attaches to a policy to add, subtract or modify coverage and takes precedence over the policy's original provisions.
facts.quote: A rider takes precedence over the original provisions in the policy

items.stem: If a rider attached to a life policy conflicts with one of the policy's original provisions, which controls?
items.explanation: Per Alaska Division of Insurance, Life Insurance Considerations, a rider is a written agreement that adds, subtracts or modifies coverage, and it takes precedence over the original provisions of the policy.

facts.statement: A family rider provides term insurance on all or certain family members under the insured's policy.
facts.quote: A family rider allows you to provide term insurance on all or certain members of your family under your policy.

items.stem: A family rider added to a parent's life policy usually provides what kind of coverage on the other family members?
items.explanation: Per Alaska Division of Insurance, Life Insurance Considerations, a family rider allows term insurance on all or certain family members under the policy.

facts.statement: The guaranteed insurability option may suit someone with a family history of significant medical problems who cannot yet afford a larger death benefit.
facts.quote: This rider may be of value to those with a family history of significant medical problems who currently have limited income and cannot afford a larger death benefit.

items.stem: A 25-year-old with a strong family history of heart disease can afford only a small policy now but expects to need much more coverage later. Which rider best protects his ability to buy that coverage?
items.explanation: Per Alaska Division of Insurance, Life Insurance Considerations, the guaranteed insurability option allows buying more death benefit at stated times without evidence of insurability, which may help someone with a family history of significant medical problems and limited current income.

facts.statement: For coverage on an other insured (such as a spouse or child rider), the form must describe what happens at the primary insured's death; if the coverage ends, unearned premium must be returned or coverage continued for the period paid.
facts.quote: If coverage on the other insured terminates upon the death of the primary insured, then the form shall provide for the return of the unearned premium

items.stem: A parent's life policy includes a rider covering the parent's spouse. The rider says the spouse's coverage ends when the parent dies. The parent dies midway through a paid premium period. Under New Jersey rules, the policy must:
options: Refund the unearned premium, or keep the coverage for the paid period
Pay the spouse's face amount to the estate right away
Convert the spouse coverage to whole life automatically
End the spouse coverage at once, with no refund at all
items.explanation: N.J.A.C. 11:4-41.9(a)1-3 requires a form that ends other-insured coverage at the primary insured's death to return the unearned premium, or else continue the coverage for the remainder of the period paid for.

facts.statement: Coverage on an other insured may be continued after the primary insured's death by waiver of premium.
facts.quote: The form may continue the coverage on the other insured by waiver of premium

items.stem: Under New Jersey rules, which is one permitted way for a policy to keep a child rider in force after the primary insured parent dies?
options: Waiving the premium for the child coverage
Raising the child coverage to the parent's face amount
Requiring the child to prove insurability again
Paying the child coverage's face amount to the estate
items.explanation: N.J.A.C. 11:4-41.9(a)1-3 permits a form to continue coverage on the other insured by waiver of premium, or by other permitted methods such as paid-up term.

facts.statement: A nursing home waiver of annuity surrender charges is limited to confinement of the owner, the annuitant, or the owner's or annuitant's spouse or civil union partner.
facts.quote: Confinement of any other family member not identified in the contract shall not qualify for the benefit.

items.stem: An annuity has a nursing home waiver of surrender charges. The contract names no other family members. Whose nursing home confinement would qualify for the waiver under New Jersey rules?
items.explanation: N.J.A.C. 11:4-43.6 limits the nursing home waiver to confinement of the owner, the annuitant, or the owner's or annuitant's spouse or civil union partner. Other family members do not qualify.

facts.statement: A terminal illness waiver of surrender charges may not require that the condition first appear or be diagnosed after the contract is issued.
facts.quote: The form shall not require that the cause of the terminal condition first manifest itself or be diagnosed after issuance of the policy or rider

items.stem: An annuity owner had early-stage cancer when she bought the contract. Years later it becomes terminal, and she asks the insurer to waive surrender charges under the terminal illness waiver. Under New Jersey rules, the insurer:
options: May deny the waiver, since the condition existed at issue
May deny the waiver unless cancer is a listed disease
May approve it only if a doctor it chooses agrees, at her cost
May not deny the waiver because the condition existed at issue
items.explanation: N.J.A.C. 11:4-43.6 bars terminal illness waivers from requiring that the condition first manifest or be diagnosed after issue, bars limiting them to specified diseases, and requires any second or third opinion to be at the insurer's expense.
items.retired: Consumer-favorable answer guessable by fairness instinct.

facts.statement: Any second or third medical opinion an insurer requires to confirm terminal illness for a surrender charge waiver must be at the insurer's expense.
facts.quote: any requirements for a second or third medical opinion to confirm the terminal illness shall be at the insurer's expense

items.stem: When a New Jersey annuity's terminal illness waiver lets the insurer require a second medical opinion, who pays for that opinion?
items.explanation: N.J.A.C. 11:4-43.6 requires the form to state that any second or third medical opinion to confirm terminal illness is at the insurer's expense.
items.retired: Consumer-favorable answer guessable by fairness instinct.

facts.statement: An annuity may not later recover a surrender charge that it waived for confinement, terminal illness or a penalty-free withdrawal.
facts.quote: shall not provide for retroactive assessment of a surrender charge to recover any prior surrender charge which was waived

items.stem: An insurer waived a $3,000 surrender charge when an annuity owner entered a nursing home. A year later she recovers and surrenders the rest of the contract. Under New Jersey rules, may the insurer add back the $3,000 it waived?
options: No, once waived it cannot be added back
Yes, if the contract is still in its surrender period
Yes, but spread over the remaining surrender years
items.explanation: N.J.A.C. 11:4-43.6 bars any retroactive assessment of a surrender charge to recover a charge previously waived for confinement, terminal illness or a penalty-free withdrawal.
items.retired: Consumer-favorable answer guessable by fairness instinct.
